title: Idaho Civics & Government (12th Grade)
description: Idaho Civics & Government (12th Grade) practice - 100 questions

questions.question: A Boise teacher asks her class what the Constitution's opening phrase 'We the People' was meant to replace as the source of authority. Under the theory those words announce, legitimate government power ultimately rests with:
questions.correctAnswer: The governed - the people, who delegate power through the Constitution
distractors: The king, ruling by divine right
The army, which enforces the laws
questions.explanation: Popular sovereignty means authority originates with the people; governments hold only the power the people grant, a break from the divine-right theory the Revolution rejected.
questions.memoryHook: T-Rexy says: Power starts with the people.

img.scene: An old parchment document resting on a wooden desk beside a brass lamp, warm window light. No readable text, no words, no letters, no numbers anywhere in the image.
img.tip: T-Rexy says: Power starts with the people.
img.title: WE THE PEOPLE

questions.question: At a Meridian town hall, a resident says the city council works for the voters, not the other way around. The principle she is describing - that government authority flows upward from ordinary citizens - is called:
questions.explanation: Popular sovereignty places the people as the source of all governmental power; officials are their agents, removable through elections and bound by constitutions the people ordain.
questions.memoryHook: T-Rexy says: The people are the boss.

img.scene: Citizens speaking with officials across a table at a small town hall meeting, friendly mood. No readable text, no words, no letters, no numbers anywhere in the image.
img.tip: T-Rexy says: The people are the boss.
img.title: POPULAR SOVEREIGNTY

questions.question: Under the Articles of Confederation, Congress needed money to pay war debts but could only ask the states to contribute voluntarily. The structural weakness this exposed was that Congress had no power to:
questions.correctAnswer: Levy taxes directly on the people
questions.explanation: The Articles gave Congress war, treaty, and postal powers, but taxation stayed with the states, whose requisitions often went unpaid - the flaw that drove calls for a stronger union.
questions.memoryHook: T-Rexy says: No tax power crippled the Articles.

img.scene: A nearly empty treasury chest in a colonial-era meeting room, candles burning low. No readable text, no words, no letters, no numbers anywhere in the image.
img.tip: T-Rexy says: No tax power crippled the Articles.
img.title: ARTICLES OF CONFEDERATION

questions.question: In 1786, indebted Massachusetts farmers shut down courthouses to stop farm foreclosures. National leaders read this uprising - Shays' Rebellion - mainly as proof that:
questions.correctAnswer: The Confederation government was too weak to keep order and protect property
distractors: The state militias were too strong
Taxes under the Articles were too high
The new nation needed a king
questions.explanation: Shays' Rebellion showed the Confederation could neither raise forces reliably nor calm domestic unrest, strengthening the movement that produced the Philadelphia Convention of 1787.
questions.memoryHook: T-Rexy says: Shays showed the cracks.

img.scene: Colonial-era farmers gathered outside a stone courthouse on a cold morning, somber mood. No readable text, no words, no letters, no numbers anywhere in the image.
img.tip: T-Rexy says: Shays showed the cracks.
img.title: SHAYS REBELLION

questions.question: When delegates gathered in Philadelphia in the summer of 1787, the task Congress had actually charged them with was to:
distractors: Draw the boundaries of the western states
questions.explanation: The delegates were called to amend the Articles; once assembled they concluded revision was not enough and drafted an entirely new Constitution instead.
questions.memoryHook: T-Rexy says: Called to revise, they rewrote.

img.scene: Men in 1700s dress debating around a long green table in a brick assembly room. No readable text, no words, no letters, no numbers anywhere in the image.
img.tip: T-Rexy says: Called to revise, they rewrote.
img.title: PHILADELPHIA 1787

questions.question: At the convention, Idaho-sized small states backed the New Jersey Plan while large states backed the Virginia Plan. The core dispute between the two plans was whether representation in Congress should be:
questions.correctAnswer: Equal for every state, or proportional to population
distractors: Limited to landowners, or open to all men
questions.explanation: Virginia wanted seats by population in both houses; New Jersey insisted on state equality. The Connecticut Compromise split the question - proportional House, equal Senate.
questions.memoryHook: T-Rexy says: Equal or by population - that was the fight.

img.scene: Two groups of delegates facing each other across a convention table, maps spread between them, no labels. No readable text, no words, no letters, no numbers anywhere in the image.
img.tip: T-Rexy says: Equal or by population - that was the fight.
img.title: TWO PLANS

questions.question: The Three-Fifths Compromise counted three-fifths of a state's enslaved population when apportioning seats and direct taxes. Its immediate purpose inside the convention was to settle how enslaved people would figure in:
questions.correctAnswer: Representation in the House (and the electoral votes tied to it)
distractors: The size of the federal judiciary
questions.explanation: Southern states wanted enslaved people counted fully for seats but not for taxes; Northern states the reverse. The 3/5 formula was the bargain struck - a moral failure that nonetheless shaped House power for decades.
questions.memoryHook: T-Rexy says: Three-fifths bought agreement, at a price.

img.scene: Delegates studying a large tally sheet by candlelight at a convention table, faces grave, sheet blank. No readable text, no words, no letters, no numbers anywhere in the image.
img.tip: T-Rexy says: Three-fifths bought agreement, at a price.
img.title: THREE-FIFTHS COMPROMISE

questions.question: Eighty-five essays urging New York to ratify the Constitution appeared in newspapers under the single pen name 'Publius.' The essayists behind that name - Hamilton, Madison, and Jay - produced the work known today as:
questions.explanation: The Federalist Papers (1787-88) remain the most influential contemporary explanation of the Constitution's design, written to win ratification in New York.
questions.memoryHook: T-Rexy says: Publius argued for ratification.

img.scene: A stack of freshly printed newspapers beside an 18th century press, ink pots nearby. No readable text, no words, no letters, no numbers anywhere in the image.
img.tip: T-Rexy says: Publius argued for ratification.
img.title: THE FEDERALIST PAPERS

questions.question: Opponents of ratification in 1788 kept returning to one omission in the proposed Constitution. The Anti-Federalists' central demand - later answered by the first ten amendments - was for:
questions.correctAnswer: An explicit bill of rights limiting the new federal government
distractors: A president elected by state legislatures
A ban on standing armies in peacetime
questions.explanation: Anti-Federalists feared a distant national government; their pressure produced the promise of a bill of rights, added in 1791 as the first ten amendments.
questions.memoryHook: T-Rexy says: No rights list, no deal.

img.scene: A speaker addressing a crowd from statehouse steps in colonial dress, listeners debating. No readable text, no words, no letters, no numbers anywhere in the image.
img.tip: T-Rexy says: No rights list, no deal.
img.title: ANTI-FEDERALIST DEMAND

questions.question: A civics diagram of the Constitution shows Article I building a legislature, Article II an executive, and Article III a judiciary. Assigning the great powers of government to three distinct branches in this way is the structural principle called:
questions.explanation: Separation of powers divides lawmaking, execution, and judging among different hands so that no single body holds the whole machinery of government; federalism, by contrast, divides power between levels.
questions.memoryHook: T-Rexy says: Three branches, three jobs.

img.scene: Three stone columns of different styles supporting one shared roof beam, symbolic. No readable text, no words, no letters, no numbers anywhere in the image.
img.tip: T-Rexy says: Three branches, three jobs.
img.title: THREE BRANCHES

questions.question: Congress passes a bill over a Boise veterans' group's objections, and the President returns it unsigned with his objections written out. The President's action is the veto - which branch-checking tool, usable only against the legislative branch?
questions.correctAnswer: A check the executive holds over Congress
distractors: A check the judiciary holds over Congress
A check Congress holds over itself
A power reserved to the states
questions.explanation: Checks and balances arm each branch against the others: the veto checks Congress, and Congress can answer with a two-thirds override in both houses.
questions.memoryHook: T-Rexy says: The veto checks Congress.

img.scene: A large document on a desk with a fountain pen set down beside it unsigned, capitol dome through the window. No readable text, no words, no letters, no numbers anywhere in the image.
img.tip: T-Rexy says: The veto checks Congress.
img.title: CHECKS AND BALANCES

questions.question: In 1803 the Supreme Court faced a dispute over last-minute judicial commissions signed by the outgoing President. Its ruling in Marbury v. Madison mattered most because the Court claimed the authority to:
questions.correctAnswer: Refuse to enforce a law it found repugnant to the Constitution - judicial review
distractors: Set the size of its own membership
questions.explanation: Marbury grounded judicial review: a law conflicting with the Constitution is void, and it is the courts' province to say what the law is. The Court used the power sparingly for decades afterward.
questions.memoryHook: T-Rexy says: Marbury claimed judicial review.

img.scene: A judge in early 1800s dress reading a commission paper at a high wooden bench. No readable text, no words, no letters, no numbers anywhere in the image.
img.tip: T-Rexy says: Marbury claimed judicial review.
img.title: MARBURY V MADISON

questions.question: A Twin Falls class traces a proposed amendment's road through Article V. Congress proposes it, and then the amendment joins the Constitution only when it is ratified by:
distractors: All of the states without exception
questions.explanation: Article V demands supermajorities at both ends: two-thirds of Congress (or a convention) to propose, three-fourths of the states - 38 of 50 - to ratify.
questions.memoryHook: T-Rexy says: Propose by two-thirds, ratify by three-fourths.

img.scene: Hands placing a sealed envelope into a large wooden ballot-style box in a statehouse hall. No readable text, no words, no letters, no numbers anywhere in the image.
img.tip: T-Rexy says: Propose by two-thirds, ratify by three-fourths.
img.title: SEALED ENVELOPE INTO A BOX

questions.question: An Idaho Falls newspaper prints a harsh editorial accusing the governor of corruption, and no official may lawfully shut the paper down for it. The protection at work is the First Amendment's guarantee of:
distractors: The right to a jury trial
questions.explanation: The First Amendment bars government from abridging press freedom; officials who dislike coverage must answer it with argument, not suppression - libel, proved in court, is a separate matter.
questions.memoryHook: T-Rexy says: The press prints, officials respond.

img.scene: A morning newspaper being read at a diner counter, coffee beside it, headline area blank. No readable text, no words, no letters, no numbers anywhere in the image.
img.tip: T-Rexy says: The press prints, officials respond.
img.title: FREEDOM OF THE PRESS

questions.question: Two clauses of the First Amendment pull in opposite directions in school-prayer disputes. The clause that stops a public school from sponsoring an official prayer is the Establishment Clause; the clause that protects a student's own private prayer is the:
questions.explanation: Establishment forbids government sponsorship of religion; Free Exercise protects private religious practice. The same amendment supplies both sides of the school-prayer cases.
questions.memoryHook: T-Rexy says: One clause stops sponsorship, one protects practice.

img.scene: A balance scale with a schoolhouse on one side and a small chapel on the other, level in soft light. No readable text, no words, no letters, no numbers anywhere in the image.
img.tip: T-Rexy says: One clause stops sponsorship, one protects practice.
img.title: TWO RELIGION CLAUSES

questions.question: A rancher outside Salmon keeps rifles for hunting and for defending his ranch. When a proposed federal rule is challenged as infringing the right 'to keep and bear Arms,' the amendment the challenge rests on is:
questions.explanation: The Second Amendment protects an individual right to possess firearms for traditionally lawful purposes, as the Supreme Court read it in District of Columbia v. Heller (2008).
questions.memoryHook: T-Rexy says: Second Amendment: keep and bear arms.

img.scene: A hunting rifle resting safely in a wooden rack inside a ranch cabin, morning light. No readable text, no words, no letters, no numbers anywhere in the image.
img.tip: T-Rexy says: Second Amendment: keep and bear arms.
img.title: SECOND AMENDMENT

questions.question: Detectives in Boise believe stolen goods are hidden in a suspect's garage, but no judge has been consulted. Under the Fourth Amendment they generally must first obtain:
questions.correctAnswer: A warrant, on probable cause, particularly describing the place to be searched and the things to be seized
distractors: A warrant signed by the police chief
questions.explanation: The Fourth Amendment conditions searches on warrants issued by a neutral judge, supported by probable cause and particular description; exceptions exist, but the warrant is the rule.
questions.memoryHook: T-Rexy says: No warrant, no search - that is the rule.

img.scene: A judge's desk with a gavel and an unsigned document beside it, courthouse window behind. No readable text, no words, no letters, no numbers anywhere in the image.
img.tip: T-Rexy says: No warrant, no search - that is the rule.
img.title: FOURTH AMENDMENT

questions.question: A highway widening near Twin Falls will take a strip of a farmer's field. The Fifth Amendment allows the taking for this public use only if the government pays the farmer:
distractors: One dollar as a token payment
Compensation only if the farmer is a veteran
questions.explanation: The Takings Clause permits eminent domain for public use with just compensation - the owner must be made whole, usually at fair market value, even though the sale cannot be refused.
questions.memoryHook: T-Rexy says: Public use requires just compensation.

img.scene: Survey stakes and ribbon marking a strip across the edge of a green farm field beside a highway. No readable text, no words, no letters, no numbers anywhere in the image.
img.tip: T-Rexy says: Public use requires just compensation.
img.title: JUST COMPENSATION

questions.question: At trial, a Pocatello defendant insists on facing the witnesses against her and questioning them herself through her lawyer. The Sixth Amendment right she is invoking is the right to:
distractors: A trial delayed as long as she wishes
Choose the judge who hears her case
questions.explanation: The Confrontation Clause guarantees the accused the chance to test accusers face to face; the same amendment adds speedy trial, impartial jury, notice of charges, and counsel.
questions.memoryHook: T-Rexy says: Face your accusers.

img.scene: An empty witness chair in a courtroom with a defendant's table facing it. No readable text, no words, no letters, no numbers anywhere in the image.
img.tip: T-Rexy says: Face your accusers.
img.title: CONFRONTATION

questions.question: A jury fines a first-time offender ten million dollars for a minor paperwork offense, and sets bail on a minor charge at fifty million. The Eighth Amendment objection that fits BOTH punishments is the ban on:
questions.correctAnswer: Excessive bail and excessive fines, and cruel and unusual punishments
questions.explanation: The Eighth Amendment limits the financial and physical penalties government may impose: bail and fines must not be excessive, and punishments must not be cruel and unusual.
questions.memoryHook: T-Rexy says: Eighth Amendment: penalties have limits.

img.scene: A courtroom scale weighed down absurdly on one side by an oversized money bag, symbolic. No readable text, no words, no letters, no numbers anywhere in the image.
img.tip: T-Rexy says: Eighth Amendment: penalties have limits.
img.title: EIGHTH AMENDMENT

questions.question: A lawyer argues that Americans hold a right to travel between states even though no clause lists it in so many words. She rests the argument on the amendment that says listing certain rights must not be read to deny others retained by the people - the:
questions.explanation: The Ninth Amendment answers the fear that a written list would shrink liberty: the people's rights are broader than the enumeration, and unlisted rights are retained, not surrendered.
questions.memoryHook: T-Rexy says: Unlisted rights are still rights.

img.scene: An open book with several blank pages following the written ones, on a library table. No readable text, no words, no letters, no numbers anywhere in the image.
img.tip: T-Rexy says: Unlisted rights are still rights.
img.title: NINTH AMENDMENT

questions.question: Idaho, not Washington, sets the rules for getting an Idaho driver's license and runs Idaho's public schools. Powers like these sit with the states because the Tenth Amendment reserves to the states or the people all powers:
questions.correctAnswer: Not delegated to the federal government nor prohibited to the states
distractors: Listed in the Bill of Rights
questions.explanation: The Tenth Amendment states the federalism default; licensing, schools, and most day-to-day governance are reserved state powers, which is exactly why state civics has its own content.
questions.memoryHook: T-Rexy says: Reserved powers run daily life.

img.scene: A state capitol dome in the foreground with a distant national capitol small behind it, symbolic. No readable text, no words, no letters, no numbers anywhere in the image.
img.tip: T-Rexy says: Reserved powers run daily life.
img.title: TENTH AMENDMENT

questions.question: It took a constitutional amendment - not merely a wartime proclamation - to end slavery permanently in every state, including on Idaho's future soil. That amendment, ratified in December 1865, was the:
questions.explanation: The Emancipation Proclamation freed enslaved people only in rebellious states as a war measure; the Thirteenth Amendment abolished slavery and involuntary servitude throughout the Union, except as criminal punishment.
questions.memoryHook: T-Rexy says: Thirteen ended slavery everywhere.

img.scene: Broken iron shackles resting on a plain wooden surface in quiet light. No readable text, no words, no letters, no numbers anywhere in the image.
img.tip: T-Rexy says: Thirteen ended slavery everywhere.
img.title: THIRTEENTH AMENDMENT

questions.question: A child born in a Boise hospital to parents who are citizens of another country is nevertheless a United States citizen from birth. The first sentence of the Fourteenth Amendment guarantees this through its:
questions.explanation: The Fourteenth Amendment (1868) constitutionalized birthright citizenship - all persons born or naturalized in the United States and subject to its jurisdiction are citizens - overruling Dred Scott's contrary holding.
questions.memoryHook: T-Rexy says: Born here means citizen here.

img.scene: A newborn's hospital bassinet beside a window with mountain light, soft and quiet. No readable text, no words, no letters, no numbers anywhere in the image.
img.tip: T-Rexy says: Born here means citizen here.
img.title: BIRTHRIGHT CITIZENSHIP

questions.question: An election official in 1968 tries to turn away a Black voter using a rule aimed at his race. The amendment written a century earlier to forbid exactly that denial of the vote is the:
questions.explanation: Ratified in 1870, the Fifteenth Amendment bars denying or abridging the vote on account of race, color, or previous condition of servitude; later laws like the Voting Rights Act gave it enforcement teeth.
questions.memoryHook: T-Rexy says: Fifteen: the vote cannot turn on race.

img.scene: A row of hands of many skin tones dropping ballots into one ballot box together. No readable text, no words, no letters, no numbers anywhere in the image.
img.tip: T-Rexy says: Fifteen: the vote cannot turn on race.
img.title: FIFTEENTH AMENDMENT

questions.question: A waitress in Idaho Falls notices federal income tax withheld from every paycheck, though the original Constitution made direct federal taxes awkward to levy. Congress's clear authority to tax incomes comes from the:
questions.explanation: The Sixteenth Amendment (1913) authorizes Congress to tax incomes from whatever source derived, without apportioning the tax among the states by population.
questions.memoryHook: T-Rexy says: Sixteen opened the income tax.

img.scene: A paycheck lying on a kitchen table beside a calculator and a coffee mug, no readable figures. No readable text, no words, no letters, no numbers anywhere in the image.
img.tip: T-Rexy says: Sixteen opened the income tax.
img.title: SIXTEENTH AMENDMENT

questions.question: Idaho voters choose their two U.S. senators directly at the ballot box. Before 1913 those seats were filled by the state legislature; the change to popular election was made by the:
questions.explanation: The Seventeenth Amendment (1913) transferred Senate elections from state legislatures to the people, leaving legislatures only the power to let governors fill vacancies temporarily.
questions.memoryHook: T-Rexy says: Seventeen gave Senate seats to voters.

img.scene: Voters marking ballots in a row of voting booths, backs to camera. No readable text, no words, no letters, no numbers anywhere in the image.
img.tip: T-Rexy says: Seventeen gave Senate seats to voters.
img.title: SEVENTEENTH AMENDMENT

questions.question: A President who has already won election twice announces a run for a third elected term. The Twenty-second Amendment blocks this because it limits any person to:
questions.correctAnswer: Being elected President at most twice
distractors: Running only if the Vice President declines
questions.explanation: Ratified in 1951 after Franklin Roosevelt's four elections, the Twenty-second Amendment caps election to the presidency at two, with a partial-term rule capping total service at ten years minus a day.
questions.memoryHook: T-Rexy says: Two elections, then the door closes.

img.scene: An hourglass nearly run out standing on an executive desk beside a flag. No readable text, no words, no letters, no numbers anywhere in the image.
img.tip: T-Rexy says: Two elections, then the door closes.
img.title: TWENTY-SECOND AMENDMENT

questions.question: When Richard Nixon resigned in 1973 his Vice President, Gerald Ford, had himself reached that office without any national election - nominated by the President and confirmed by Congress. The amendment supplying that vacancy procedure is the:
questions.explanation: The Twenty-fifth Amendment (1967) lets the President nominate a new Vice President when the office empties; both houses confirm. It also governs presidential disability and succession.
questions.memoryHook: T-Rexy says: Twenty-five fills the VP's chair.

img.scene: Two formal chairs in a row, the second one standing empty, draped office behind. No readable text, no words, no letters, no numbers anywhere in the image.
img.tip: T-Rexy says: Twenty-five fills the VP's chair.
img.title: TWENTY-FIFTH AMENDMENT

questions.question: A county in 1963 charges citizens a fee at the polls before letting them vote for Congress. The Twenty-fourth Amendment destroyed that device - the poll tax - but only, by its own text, for:
questions.correctAnswer: Federal elections (primaries and elections for federal office)
questions.explanation: The Twenty-fourth Amendment (1964) banned poll taxes in federal elections; the Supreme Court's Harper decision (1966) then struck state-election poll taxes under the Fourteenth Amendment.
questions.memoryHook: T-Rexy says: Twenty-four banned the federal poll tax.

img.scene: A coin slot on an old wooden ballot box, pried off and lying beside it, symbolic. No readable text, no words, no letters, no numbers anywhere in the image.
img.tip: T-Rexy says: Twenty-four banned the federal poll tax.
img.title: POLL TAX

questions.question: For Idaho's two seats in the U.S. House, voters in each congressional district elect a representative who then serves a term of:
questions.explanation: House members stand for election every two years, keeping the chamber closest to shifting public opinion; senators serve six and presidents four, by contrast.
questions.memoryHook: T-Rexy says: House terms run two years.

img.scene: A campaign sign being planted in a front yard in autumn, wording on the sign blank. No readable text, no words, no letters, no numbers anywhere in the image.
img.tip: T-Rexy says: House terms run two years.
img.title: HOUSE TERMS

questions.question: Only about a third of the U.S. Senate faces the voters in any single election year. That pattern exists because Senate terms are six years long and:
questions.correctAnswer: Staggered, so the terms of the classes expire in rotation
distractors: Renewed only when a seat falls vacant
questions.explanation: The Constitution divides senators into three classes with staggered six-year terms, giving the Senate continuity - it never turns over entirely at one election.
questions.memoryHook: T-Rexy says: Six-year terms, staggered in thirds.

img.scene: Three rows of desks in a senate chamber, one row lit brightly and the others dim, symbolic. No readable text, no words, no letters, no numbers anywhere in the image.
img.tip: T-Rexy says: Six-year terms, staggered in thirds.
img.title: STAGGERED SENATE

questions.question: A 27-year-old from Nampa asks which federal offices she is already old enough to hold. The Constitution's age floors are 25 for the House, 30 for the Senate, and 35 for the presidency, so at 27 she qualifies for:
questions.correctAnswer: The U.S. House of Representatives only
questions.explanation: Age is only part of it - the House also requires seven years' citizenship and residence in the state - but 27 clears just one of the three age bars.
questions.memoryHook: T-Rexy says: Twenty-five, thirty, thirty-five.

img.scene: Three ascending steps leading to three doors of increasing size, symbolic. No readable text, no words, no letters, no numbers anywhere in the image.
img.tip: T-Rexy says: Twenty-five, thirty, thirty-five.
img.title: AGE FLOORS

questions.question: A bill raising taxes is introduced first in the Senate, and a point of order is raised against it. The Origination Clause of Article I requires that bills for raising revenue begin in:
distractors: A joint committee of both houses
questions.explanation: Revenue bills start in the chamber elected directly and most frequently by the people; the Senate may still amend them, as it did even under this clause.
questions.memoryHook: T-Rexy says: Tax bills are born in the House.

img.scene: A document being carried from a larger chamber doorway toward a smaller one down a marble hall. No readable text, no words, no letters, no numbers anywhere in the image.
img.tip: T-Rexy says: Tax bills are born in the House.
img.title: ORIGINATION CLAUSE

questions.question: A federal judge is impeached by the House and put on trial. Removal from office, if it comes, requires a two-thirds vote of the body conducting the trial - which is:
questions.explanation: The House impeaches by majority vote, functioning like a grand jury; the Senate tries the case, and conviction - removal - takes two-thirds of senators present.
questions.memoryHook: T-Rexy says: House charges, Senate removes or acquits.

img.scene: A solemn chamber arranged for a trial, with a presiding chair and rows of seated members. No readable text, no words, no letters, no numbers anywhere in the image.
img.tip: T-Rexy says: House charges, Senate removes or acquits.
img.title: IMPEACHMENT TRIAL

questions.question: Idaho shares a short border with Canada, and a proposed U.S.-Canada water treaty is sent to the Senate. A treaty becomes binding on the United States only with the consent of:
distractors: The governors of the border states
questions.explanation: Article II requires two-thirds Senate consent for treaties - a supermajority that makes treaties deliberately harder than ordinary statutes, which need only majorities of both houses plus a signature or override.
questions.memoryHook: T-Rexy says: Treaties need two-thirds of the Senate.

img.scene: A rolled treaty document tied with ribbon on a desk, a mountain border landscape through the window. No readable text, no words, no letters, no numbers anywhere in the image.
img.tip: T-Rexy says: Treaties need two-thirds of the Senate.
img.title: TREATY CONSENT

questions.question: Senators opposed to a bill are talking it to death on the floor. Under Senate Rule XXII, cutting off that filibuster - invoking cloture - on most legislation requires the votes of:
questions.explanation: Cloture's three-fifths threshold shapes modern lawmaking: major bills effectively need 60 Senate votes, not a simple majority, before a final vote can occur.
questions.memoryHook: T-Rexy says: Sixty ends most filibusters.

img.scene: A senator speaking at a podium piled high with papers, late-evening light in the chamber. No readable text, no words, no letters, no numbers anywhere in the image.
img.tip: T-Rexy says: Sixty ends most filibusters.
img.title: CLOTURE

questions.question: Congress charters a national bank in 1816, and Maryland tries to tax it out of existence. In McCulloch v. Maryland the Court upheld the bank using the clause that empowers Congress to make laws that are:
questions.correctAnswer: 'Necessary and proper' for executing its enumerated powers
distractors: Expressly listed word for word in Article I
Approved in advance by the states
Ratified by three-fourths of the states
questions.explanation: McCulloch read the Necessary and Proper Clause broadly: let the end be legitimate and within the Constitution, and the means Congress chooses are constitutional too.
questions.memoryHook: T-Rexy says: Necessary and proper means room to work.

img.scene: An early American bank building with columns, a state tax notice posted blank on its door. No readable text, no words, no letters, no numbers anywhere in the image.
img.tip: T-Rexy says: Necessary and proper means room to work.
img.title: MCCULLOCH V MARYLAND

questions.question: Wheat grown on an Idaho farm is trucked to a port in another state, and potatoes cross three state lines on one rail journey. Congress's power to regulate that traffic rests chiefly on its authority over:
questions.explanation: The Commerce Clause (Article I, Section 8) reaches goods moving across state lines; since Gibbons v. Ogden (1824) it has been read as a wide grant over interstate economic activity.
questions.memoryHook: T-Rexy says: Interstate commerce is Congress's beat.

img.scene: A freight train crossing a steel bridge over a wide river canyon at sunset. No readable text, no words, no letters, no numbers anywhere in the image.
img.tip: T-Rexy says: Interstate commerce is Congress's beat.
img.title: COMMERCE CLAUSE

questions.question: During a crisis abroad, a Boise enlistee asks who can actually declare war. Under the Constitution the war-declaring power belongs to Congress, while the President's distinct military role is:
questions.correctAnswer: Commander in chief of the armed forces
questions.explanation: Article I gives Congress the declaration of war and the power to raise and support armies (with two-year funding limits); Article II makes the President the forces' commander once raised.
questions.memoryHook: T-Rexy says: Congress declares, the President commands.

img.scene: A president reviewing troops on a parade ground, flags above, no readable insignia text. No readable text, no words, no letters, no numbers anywhere in the image.
img.tip: T-Rexy says: Congress declares, the President commands.
img.title: DECLARE WAR

questions.question: A President issues an executive order directing federal agencies how to enforce a statute. The order carries legal weight only insofar as it traces back to:
questions.correctAnswer: The Constitution or an act of Congress
distractors: A majority vote of the Cabinet
questions.explanation: Executive orders are instructions for executing existing law; they cannot create law from nothing, and courts strike orders that exceed the President's constitutional or statutory authority.

questions.question: A Boise voter faces a long executive-branch ballot: governor, lieutenant governor, secretary of state, state controller, state treasurer, attorney general, and superintendent of public instruction. Idaho fills all of these offices by:
questions.correctAnswer: Separate election - a plural executive, not appointment by the governor
distractors: Appointment by the state supreme court
questions.explanation: Idaho voters elect their executive team member by member; the governor cannot fire the independently elected attorney general or superintendent, a design that fragments executive power on purpose.

questions.question: At the head of every Idaho county sits an elected board that sets the county budget, maintains county roads, and supervises other county officers. Statewide, that governing body is the:
questions.correctAnswer: Board of County Commissioners (three elected commissioners)
distractors: County mayor and council of nine
questions.explanation: Three commissioners, elected from districts within the county, form the board - Idaho counties have no single county executive; authority is shared with the other elected row officers.

questions.explanation: The sheriff is an elected county officer in Idaho, running the county jail and serving as its chief law enforcer outside city police jurisdictions - an office that answers to voters, not to the commissioners.

questions.question: Standard GOV.44 directs Idaho students to tribal sovereignty 'with emphasis on Idaho,' including hunting and fishing rights and land leasing. Sovereignty, for the five federally recognized tribes in Idaho, means the tribes are:

questions.explanation: Tribal sovereignty is inherent and retained, not granted by Idaho; the state cannot simply legislate over tribal governments, which is why treaties and federal law frame hunting, fishing, and leasing questions.

questions.explanation: Fort Hall, created by an 1868 treaty-era executive order along the Snake River plain, is home to the Shoshone and Bannock peoples jointly - the Shoshone-Bannock Tribes.

questions.question: In the Treaty of 1855, the Nez Perce reserved - kept for themselves - the right to hunt, fish, and gather on lands they ceded to the United States. When Idaho students study those reserved rights today (GOV.44), the key idea is that a treaty cession:
questions.correctAnswer: Transferred some rights while the tribes expressly retained others, which remain in force
distractors: Erased every tribal right on the ceded land
Applied only while the signers lived
questions.explanation: Reserved-rights doctrine: tribes gave up title to most of the land but kept hunting, fishing, and gathering rights on it - rights the Supreme Court has repeatedly treated as surviving statehood.
questions.memoryHook: T-Rexy says: Reserved means kept, not given away.

questions.question: Standard GOV.46 asks students to compare how laws are made at the national, state, and local levels. One method exists ONLY at the state-and-local side of that comparison in Idaho: Idaho voters, by gathering petition signatures, can place a proposed law on the ballot themselves - the power of:
questions.explanation: Idaho's constitution has allowed the initiative since voters added it in 1912: a petition signed by enough electors sends a proposed statute straight to the ballot, bypassing the legislature.
questions.memoryHook: T-Rexy says: Voters can legislate: the initiative.

questions.question: Companion to the initiative, Idaho's referendum power lets voters do the reverse - take a law the legislature has just passed and, by petition, send it to the ballot for the people to:
distractors: Amend its wording line by line
Send it to the Supreme Court
questions.explanation: Where the initiative starts a law with the people, the referendum is the people's veto: timely petitions suspend a new statute until voters sustain or kill it at the next election.
questions.memoryHook: T-Rexy says: The referendum is the people's veto.
